name: Subcutaneous testosterone injection

lead: Subcutaneous testosterone injection delivers testosterone esters into the fat layer under the skin instead of deep into a muscle. It is a route of testosterone replacement therapy, and a weekly subcutaneous auto-injector of testosterone enanthate (Xyosted) is a marketed product.

For appearance, the appeal is the same as testosterone therapy in general: restoring levels in men with low testosterone is associated with more lean mass, less fat and better energy for training. People who prefer subcutaneous injections cite smaller needles and easier self-administration.

paras: Under medical supervision, a clinician prescribes the formulation and schedule and monitors blood tests. Forum users describe more frequent small injections and discuss comfort, lumps and bloodwork; these accounts are anecdotes, and dosing is individualised by prescribers.

Testosterone therapy can raise hematocrit, and a 2019 forum-discussed study linked injection frequency and testosterone level to polycythemia. Other documented effects include acne, gynecomastia, suppressed fertility and, since February 2025, a blood pressure warning on US labels. Injection-site reactions such as lumps or swelling are reported.

angle.text: Testosterone is an anabolic hormone, and replacement therapy is used to restore levels in men with low testosterone. The subcutaneous route changes how the hormone is delivered rather than what it does; users discuss it as a more convenient way to self-administer.

lead: Subcutaneous testosterone injection (often called SubQ TRT) is the administration of an injectable testosterone ester into the fat under the skin rather than into a muscle. Intramuscular injection is described as the most common route of testosterone therapy, while subcutaneous options include the weekly auto-injector Xyosted (testosterone enanthate) and Testopel implantable pellets [1].

People use testosterone replacement to improve muscle, fat loss, energy and drive, which in turn shape physique. In forums such as T Nation, members on prescribed TRT compare subcutaneous and intramuscular routes, often citing smaller needles and a view that smaller, more frequent injections smooth hormone levels [2][3]. A published retrospective cohort of 22 transgender men found that weekly subcutaneous testosterone cypionate raised serum testosterone into the target range over six months [4].

paras: Testosterone esters such as cypionate and enanthate act as prodrugs that release testosterone after injection [1]. Intramuscular injection is the most common route, but subcutaneous administration into abdominal or thigh fat is used with auto-injectors and by some patients who self-inject [1][4].
Wikipedia lists Xyosted as an auto-injector of testosterone enanthate given once weekly, and Testopel as a pellet implanted under the skin every 3 to 6 months [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and TRT communities
paras: On T Nation, members on prescribed therapy compare routes. One long-term user describes starting subcutaneous shots twice weekly on the understanding that this would slow release and smooth peaks, then reports a mixed experience with pain, swelling and lumps [2]. Another thread contains a user reporting a strong initial effect on mood and energy when starting daily subcutaneous injections, while questioning how much might be placebo [5].

Threads also discuss bloodwork after switching routes, with posters reporting different results on the same weekly amount; others argue that studies show little difference in absorption between routes [6]. These are individual accounts.

Wikipedia notes that raised hematocrit is a common effect requiring monitoring, with levels above 54 percent an absolute contraindication and above 50 percent a relative one. Injectables can cause pulmonary oil microembolism, and the FDA has added warnings on deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Acne, oily skin and gynecomastia are also reported [1].

A T Nation thread discusses a study that found polycythemia associated with testosterone level and age, with an odds ratio of 24.7 for log testosterone, and that injection frequency indicated risk [7]. In February 2025, FDA label changes removed language on increased cardiovascular risk from the boxed warning and added a warning about blood pressure increases [1].

A 2026 retrospective cohort in the Indian Journal of Endocrinology and Metabolism followed 22 transgender men given weekly subcutaneous testosterone cypionate for six months. Average testosterone rose significantly and estradiol fell to a mean of about 46.6 pg/mL, with the authors concluding the route was effective and convenient [4]. The cohort was small and retrospective.
